prompt.context: Our client is Milk & Cheese, Inc. (MCI), a consumer goods company in the food sector with a portfolio of 1,000+ products. MCI is experiencing profitability challenges. Another team in your firm is already working on costs and expenses. Your team is focusing on the MCI product portfolio.
prompt.question: Your role is to analyze which, if any, products MCI should stop producing/selling. How would you do that?

clarifying_info.q: Is SG&A affected by any potential portfolio changes?
clarifying_info.a: No, SG&A is not affected by the potential changes.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average volume across products?
What is the average margin across products?

framework: Identify all products in MCI portfolio (1,000+ SKUs)
For each product, obtain margin (%) and volume (tons)
Plot products on a scatter plot with margin on one axis and volume on the other
Use averages (margin 16%, volume 35k tons) as axis dividers to create four quadrants
Identify low-margin, low-volume products (quadrant D) as candidates for elimination
Apply Pareto (80/20) analysis to confirm which products drive 80% of profit
Evaluate options for problem products: discontinue, sell to competitors, or investigate turnaround potential
Assess risks of each option before making a recommendation

questions.prompt: How would you structure the analysis to identify which products to cut from a 1,000+ product portfolio?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize that with 1,000+ products, a spreadsheet-based approach is needed. Strong candidates quickly identify that you need at least two dimensions: profitability (margin) and scale (volume). They should suggest a scatter plot or a Pareto chart. The key data combinations are: Revenue + COGS, or Price + Cost/unit + Volume, or Margin + Volume, or Margin + Revenue. Margin vs. Volume is preferred for this case since prices are not materially different across products.

questions.prompt: Given average volume of 35k tons and average margin of 16%, how do you use these to segment the portfolio?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use the averages as axis dividers on the scatter plot, creating four quadrants: A (high margin, high volume) = star products; B (high margin, low volume) = niche profitable; C (low margin, high volume) = scale-dependent; D (low margin, low volume) = candidates for elimination. On the Pareto chart, products in Category I drive 80% of cumulative profit; Category II products (approx. 200) contribute little to profit and are problematic.

math.setup: Use average margin (16%) and average volume (35k tons) as cut-off lines on scatter plot axes.
steps: Divide scatter plot into 4 quadrants using averages as boundaries
Zone A: above-average margin AND above-average volume — core products
Zone B: above-average margin, below-average volume — niche but profitable
Zone C: below-average margin, above-average volume — investigate cost reduction
Zone D: below-average margin AND below-average volume — elimination candidates (~200 products)
On Pareto: top ~20% of products (Category I) drive ~80% of profit; remaining ~80% (Category II, ~200+ products) contribute minimally
math.answer: Approximately 200 products fall in Zone D (low margin, low volume) and are primary targets for removal from the portfolio.

brainstorming.prompt: What options does MCI have for dealing with the ~200 low-margin, low-volume products identified in Zone D?

categories.name: Discontinue
ideas: Phase out gradually to avoid customer disruption
Redirect manufacturing capacity to higher-margin products

categories.name: Divest / Sell
ideas: Sell product lines to smaller regional competitors
Bundle with other low performers for a portfolio sale

categories.name: Turnaround / Empower
ideas: Investigate root causes of low margin (pricing too low, costs too high)
Explore price increases if products have loyal niche customer base
Find cost reduction opportunities in production or procurement

categories.name: Monitor
ideas: Retain products with strategic value (e.g., entry-level SKU that drives upsell)
Keep products required by key retail customers as part of shelf assortment agreements

recommendation: Based on the portfolio analysis, approximately 200 products fall into Zone D — below-average margin and below-average volume — and are not contributing meaningfully to MCI's profitability.
MCI should consider removing these products from its portfolio, either by discontinuing production or by selling them to minor competitors.
risks: Selling Zone D products to major competitors could jeopardize MCI's core business by strengthening rivals
Some Zone D products may serve as entry-level or complementary SKUs that anchor customer relationships; removing them could have downstream revenue effects
Supply chain and manufacturing disruptions during transition if capacity is not reallocated efficiently
Reputational or retail relationship risk if key accounts expect full product breadth
next_steps: Conduct detailed review of each Zone D product for strategic exceptions before cutting
Model margin improvement potential for Zone C (low margin, high volume) products
Assess buyer appetite among minor competitors for divested SKUs
Develop a phased portfolio rationalization plan with timeline and milestones
